title: One pod calls another: the whole packet path
subtitle: DNS, a virtual IP that nothing listens on, and the kernel
scenario:
A pod in namespace `prod` runs `curl http://api/health`. There are three `api` pods, on three different nodes.

Nothing anywhere is listening on the Service IP. There is no proxy process in the path. Follow the packet and see what actually moves it.

steps.title: `api` is not a name yet

ask.prompt: The caller is in namespace `prod`. What does its resolver actually query first for the bare name `api`?
choices: api.prod.svc.cluster.local — the first search domain from /etc/resolv.conf
api — sent as-is, because it is a valid hostname
ask.explain: The kubelet writes the search list into every pod's resolv.conf, own namespace first. This is why `api` reaches a Service in your own namespace but you need `api.payments` to reach one next door.

steps.body:
The kubelet wrote `/etc/resolv.conf` when the pod started. It points at the CoreDNS Service and lists search domains, own namespace first.

The `ndots:5` line matters more than it looks: any name with fewer than 5 dots gets tried against every search domain **before** being tried as-is. Great for short in-cluster names, expensive for external ones — `api.github.com` costs three failed lookups before the real one.

code.label: inside the calling pod
code.text:
$ cat /etc/resolv.conf
nameserver 10.43.0.10
search prod.svc.cluster.local svc.cluster.local cluster.local
options ndots:5

$ nslookup api
Name:    api.prod.svc.cluster.local
Address: 10.43.12.201

steps.title: A name becomes a virtual IP
steps.body:
CoreDNS answers with the Service's **ClusterIP**: `10.43.12.201`.

Notice what it did *not* return. Not a pod IP, not a list of pod IPs, not a node address. One stable virtual IP that will outlive every pod behind it.

(The exception is a headless Service — `clusterIP: None` — where DNS returns the pod IPs directly. That is what StatefulSets use, so you can address `postgres-0` specifically.)

code.label: the two flavors, side by side
code.text:
$ kubectl get svc api postgres
NAME       TYPE        CLUSTER-IP     PORT(S)
api        ClusterIP   10.43.12.201   80/TCP
postgres   ClusterIP   None           5432/TCP

$ nslookup postgres
Address: 10.42.1.9      # the pod itself
Address: 10.42.2.4

steps.watch: If a name resolves but connections hang, DNS has done its job — stop looking there and go to endpoints or NetworkPolicy.

steps.title: The packet leaves, addressed to nothing

choices: Nothing. No process anywhere binds a ClusterIP
kube-proxy, which accepts and forwards the connection
The CoreDNS pod, acting as a proxy
One of the api pods, which claims the IP
ask.explain: A ClusterIP is a fiction maintained by the kernel. Nothing answers ARP for it and nothing binds it. This is why you often cannot ping a ClusterIP, and why tcpdump on the node shows pod IPs rather than Service IPs.

steps.body:
curl opens a TCP connection to `10.43.12.201:80`. The packet leaves the pod's network namespace addressed to an IP that exists nowhere.

It does not get far before the kernel rewrites it.

code.label: the Service CIDR is not the pod CIDR
code.text:
# RKE2 defaults
#   10.42.0.0/16   pods       - real addresses on real interfaces
#   10.43.0.0/16   services   - virtual, exists only as kernel rules
code.note: Seeing 10.42.x versus 10.43.x tells you instantly whether you are looking at something real or something virtual.

steps.title: The kernel picks a backend and rewrites the address
steps.body:
On this node, kube-proxy has already written iptables (or IPVS) rules for every Service in the cluster. It did that by watching Services and **EndpointSlices** — it is not in the data path itself, it only programs it.

The rule chain for `api` matches the destination, then picks one endpoint at random and DNATs the packet to that pod's real IP.

That `--probability` line is the entire load-balancing algorithm: random, per new connection. No least-connections, no health-aware retries, no stickiness beyond what conntrack remembers.

code.label: the actual rules on the node
code.text:
$ iptables-save -t nat | grep 10.43.12.201
-A KUBE-SERVICES -d 10.43.12.201/32 -p tcp --dport 80 -j KUBE-SVC-XN3

$ iptables-save -t nat | grep KUBE-SVC-XN3
-A KUBE-SVC-XN3 -m statistic --mode random --probability 0.33333 -j KUBE-SEP-A
-A KUBE-SVC-XN3 -m statistic --mode random --probability 0.50000 -j KUBE-SEP-B
-A KUBE-SVC-XN3 -j KUBE-SEP-C

$ iptables-save -t nat | grep KUBE-SEP-A
-A KUBE-SEP-A -p tcp -j DNAT --to-destination 10.42.2.9:8080

steps.title: The packet crosses to another node
steps.body:
The destination is now `10.42.2.9`, a real pod IP on node3. The CNI moves it there — with Canal that means wrapping it in a VXLAN packet between the two node IPs, unwrapping on the far side.

This is where MTU bites. VXLAN adds about 50 bytes. If the pod MTU was not reduced to match, small packets sail through and full-size ones are silently dropped: handshakes work, large responses hang forever.

code.label: the MTU test worth memorizing
code.text:
# works: small request
$ kubectl exec -it debug -- curl -s http://api/health

# hangs: large response
$ kubectl exec -it debug -- curl -s http://api/dump

# confirm with a do-not-fragment ping just under the tunnel size
$ kubectl exec -it debug -- ping -M do -s 1422 10.42.2.9

steps.title: Two independent verdicts, not one

ask.prompt: Namespace `prod` has a default-deny egress policy. Namespace `payments` allows ingress from `prod`. Can a prod pod reach a payments pod?
choices: No — egress is judged at the source and ingress at the destination, and both must allow it
Yes — the destination's allow rule is what counts
Yes, if both namespaces share a CNI
Only for TCP; UDP is always denied
ask.explain: Two separate checks in two separate places. It is also why a default-deny egress policy that forgets UDP/TCP 53 to CoreDNS breaks every app in the namespace at once — DNS is egress traffic too.

steps.body:
If either pod is selected by a NetworkPolicy, the CNI enforces it — Calico, in Canal's case. A pod that no policy selects accepts everything; the moment one selects it, only what is explicitly allowed gets through.

Egress is evaluated at the caller, ingress at the callee, and they are completely independent. When debugging, always check both ends.

code.label: the rule people forget

steps.title: The reply finds its way home
steps.body:
The api pod replies from `10.42.2.9`. On the way back, the source node's **conntrack** table reverses the translation, so the caller sees a reply from `10.43.12.201` — the address it actually dialed.

Without that, the caller would receive a packet from an IP it never contacted and drop it. Conntrack is also why a Service connection stays pinned to one backend for its lifetime even though selection was random.

code.label: the translation, live
code.text:
$ conntrack -L | grep 10.43.12.201
tcp 6 86398 ESTABLISHED src=10.42.0.31 dst=10.43.12.201 sport=52344 dport=80
                        src=10.42.2.9 dst=10.42.0.31 sport=8080 dport=52344
code.note: Two lines: what the pod thinks it is talking to, and what is really happening.

steps.title: When it breaks, walk the same path

ask.prompt: `curl api` returns connection refused. `nslookup api` returns the ClusterIP correctly. Where do you look first?
choices: EndpointSlices — an empty one means the selector matches nothing or nothing is Ready
CoreDNS logs, since name resolution is the usual culprit
ask.explain: Resolution worked, so DNS is cleared. An empty EndpointSlice is the single most common cause and takes one command to rule in or out — and it is not really a networking problem at all, it is a labels-or-readiness problem.

steps.body:
The path gives you an ordered checklist, and each step is one command:

- **Does the name resolve?** `nslookup api` — no means CoreDNS or resolv.conf.
- **Does the Service have backends?** `kubectl get endpointslices` — empty means selector mismatch or nothing Ready.
- **Do the rules exist on the node?** `iptables-save -t nat | grep <clusterIP>`.
- **Is a policy dropping it?** Check egress at the source *and* ingress at the destination.
- **Is it only large payloads?** MTU.

Answering in that order beats guessing, every time.

code.label: the four commands, in order
code.text:
$ kubectl exec -it debug -- nslookup api
$ kubectl get endpointslices -l kubernetes.io/service-name=api
$ kubectl get pods -l app=api -o wide          # are they Ready?
$ kubectl get networkpolicy -A

takeaways: A ClusterIP has no listener. It is a kernel rewrite rule that kube-proxy programs from EndpointSlices.
Load balancing is random per connection — nothing more sophisticated is happening.
Only Ready pods are in an EndpointSlice, which is what makes the readiness probe meaningful.
DNS resolving proves DNS works. From there the fault is endpoints, policy or MTU — in that order of likelihood.
